schools.summary: Theodoret notices how much Paul passed over — the three thousand of Pentecost, the myriads James spoke of, the believing Jews scattered through the land — and instances himself instead of any of them.

Gill puts the objection in an adversary's mouth — if Israel is set aside, what becomes of the covenant with Abraham, the promises, and God's faithfulness? — and notes that the denial of any casting-off was still an article of the Jewish creed in his own day. Calvin refuses to read the tribe of Benjamin as a display of mercy toward a nearly destroyed clan, calling that forced and far-fetched, and takes the pedigree to establish only that Paul is a native Israelite and no proselyte.

Clarke derives the verb from the preposition and the verb meaning to thrust or drive, so that the question is whether God has driven Israel eternally from him; the rejection Paul repudiates is the universal and final one, not every kind.
Henry hears the argument in the first person: to say the Jews are all rejected would be for Paul to cut off his own claims and see himself abandoned.

Barnes locates the objection's flaw in a word Paul never said — that God rejected ALL his people — and lays out the five moves that dismantle it. Robertson notes the interrogative expects an indignant No and recalls the promise God made three times over. Ellicott resists the usual reading of the pedigree, taking the appeal to spring from patriotic sympathy rather than self-interest, and observes that Benjamin was of the purest blood since Judah and Benjamin alone kept the theocratic continuity after the Exile.

debates: Why Paul cites his own descent. The usual reading makes it self-interest — if all Abraham's seed are cut off, Paul is cut off; Ellicott finds that inconsistent with the generosity of a man who had wished himself accursed for his kinsmen, and reads it as patriotic sympathy.
What the tribe of Benjamin contributes. Ellicott makes it purity of blood after the Exile; Calvin rejects the reading that finds in it a display of mercy to a nearly destroyed tribe.

schools.summary: Theodoret glosses the clause as marking those who proved worthy of the divine knowledge by welcoming the light of faith, and hears in it Paul's own security, since had God cast them off he too would have stood condemned.

Calvin divides the answer: God has not cast away Abraham's race contrary to his covenant, and yet the fruit of adoption does not belong to all the children of the flesh, because a secret election runs beneath the visible people — the visible body rejected in such a way that no member of Christ's spiritual body was cut off. He denies that the participle means foresight of what a man will be, and makes it the good pleasure by which God chose the unborn. Gill argues from the other end: all mankind are in a sense God's people, but were all foreknown they would all be predestinated, called, justified and glorified.

Clarke reads the verb as loved or approved, the ordinary force of the Hebrew and Greek words for knowing, and takes the promise to be of special favour rather than of an unbreakable decree. Wesley treats the tense as accommodation, knowing and foreknowing being one thing with God, who sees all at once from everlasting.

Barnes denies it is bare foresight, finding a previous purpose in it and drawing the consequence that the truly renewed persevere; he also explains that the Old Testament was cited by subject, so IN ELIJAH means the passage that tells his story. Ellicott warns the phrase must not be pressed into an absolute indefectibility of divine favour. Robertson notes the verb for pleading is neutral in itself, the hostility carried by the preposition.

debates: What the participle for foreknowing means. Calvin and Gill take it for eternal electing good pleasure; Clarke for love or approval; Ellicott warns against pressing it into indefectibility; Wesley treats the tense as human accommodation; Theodoret makes it descriptive of those who welcomed faith.

schools.summary: Gill traces the killing of the prophets to Jezebel's order, notes that Christ and the apostles lay the same crime at that nation's door in later generations, and observes that the Kings text adds WITH THE SWORD, the clause standing elsewhere in the original by a rule of transposition.
Clarke reads the whole speech as the report of a man who believes no prophet but himself survives and that his own life is hunted.

Barnes marks the citation as free and denies Elijah's inference: that prophets were murdered proved the character of the nation but not that no godly men were left. He supplies the ritual detail behind the verb — altars of earth or unhewn stone, so that digging them down is levelling them — and fills in why the prophet could believe himself alone, the hundred hidden in a cave apparently since discovered. Lightfoot asks what altars of God stood in Samaria at all, answering from a Jewish authority that they were private altars raised to God's name, lawful before the temple was built, and indefensible afterwards only where the road to Jerusalem lay open. Ellicott trims the claim to its real extent, left alone of the prophets; Robertson notes the verb for digging under occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and that Paul reversed the order of the Greek Old Testament's clauses.

debates: Whether the northern altars were lawful. Lightfoot distinguishes by geography: private altars in Judah and Benjamin were indefensible with Jerusalem open to them, but the ten tribes had no such access, and he leaves it a question whether Elijah would have called theirs unlawful.
outliers: Barnes treats Elijah's conclusion as unfounded even though his charge was true, making the prophet's despair a mistake of inference rather than of fact.

schools.summary: Theodoret turns the episode on the reader: all of them were called Israel, God named himself the God of seven thousand, and the prophet who was one of them did not know these existed — so it is nothing new if you do not know who among you has believed.
Gill identifies the divine response with the still small voice of the history and with what the rabbis called the daughter of a voice.

Clarke takes seven as a certain figure standing for an uncertain one and explains the invisibility practically: Jezebel's persecution forced them to conceal their attachment to the true religion, and providence preserved them from her rage.

Barnes notes the noun for the oracle occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, renders the Hebrew of the reserving as I HAVE CAUSED TO REMAIN so that the honour is claimed by God and traced to nothing in the men, and turns the number into encouragement — Elijah supposed he was alone and there were thousands. Robertson points to the related verb used of the warnings given to the magi and to Simeon, and explains the feminine article from the Jewish substitution of the word for shame. Ellicott reports the same feminine gender as the reason the translators inserted the word IMAGE, leaving its origin open. Lightfoot uses the verse against those who would correct the Hebrew by the Greek, since Paul and the translators differ twice over, and doubts the arithmetic taken strictly.

debates: Whether the seven thousand is a literal count. Clarke and Barnes take seven for a round or indefinite number; Lightfoot doubts the figure taken strictly and suggests there may have been seventy thousand.

Why the idol's name carries a feminine article. Ellicott leaves the cause open, reporting the guesses that the deity was androgynous or the gender contemptuous; Robertson explains it from the substituted word for shame.
outliers: Lightfoot uses the verse polemically, against the claim that the Greek translators wrote by prophetic inspiration, since here they and Paul cannot both be right.

schools.summary: Gill fixes the present as the time of the preaching of the gospel, when the nation as a body had rejected the Messiah and persecuted the apostles, and God had still made a reserve for himself.

Clarke empties the phrase of particularity: the election of grace is God's gracious design in sending the Christian system into the world and saving under it everyone who believes and no one else. Wesley compresses the same reading into the purpose that he who believes shall be saved.

Barnes runs the parallel with Elijah's day point by point and turns it into four lessons — that declension is no new thing, that it should produce deep feeling, that it is no warrant for discouragement, and that any preservation is God's doing. Robertson notes the noun for remnant appears here alone in the New Testament. Lightfoot fastens on the time-marker and reads the argument as strictly contemporary, treating AT THIS PRESENT TIME as evidence against taking the passage for a promise of a future national call.

debates: What the election of grace is. Gill and Barnes take the reservation for a choosing that precedes and produces believing; Clarke and Wesley make it the general scheme by which God saves whoever believes.
outliers: Lightfoot dissents from the future-restoration reading the rest of the chapter is usually given, arguing from AT THIS PRESENT TIME that the remnant in view is the one being called in Paul's own age.

schools.summary: Theodoret reads the works negatively as the polity of the law, and observes that this is why salvation is itself called grace, proceeding from the divine kindness.

Gill grounds the exclusion in the timing: election passed before any works were done, and works rightly done spring from it, so they can never be its rule or condition. Calvin generalises the logic, saying Paul has gone higher than the means of salvation to why God chose some before the foundation of the world, and that it makes no difference whether the works are past or future.

Clarke accepts the antithesis but empties the election of particularity: what is denied is a sovereign act singling out some who might as easily have taken in the whole nation, and what is meant is the general scheme by which God receives anyone who believes — from which he draws that these same believers would have been excluded had they remained in unbelief, and every Jew without exception would have been taken in had they believed. Wesley extends the exclusion to works ceremonial and moral alike.

Barnes turns it into a transaction: justification by works would be debt and not favour, so salvation cannot be partly of grace and partly of works. Robertson notes the tense, that grace does not merely cease to be grace but stops becoming it. Ellicott reports that the true text differs considerably from the longer form the Authorised Version renders, while the substance survives either way.

debates: What the election of grace denotes. Calvin makes it a choice made before the world was founded; Clarke makes it the general scheme of receiving believers, and says every Jew would have been taken in had they believed.

Whether the second half of the verse is genuine. Calvin reports Griesbach judging it spurious on manuscript grounds, and defends it on style, noting that Beza, Pareus and Wolfius held it genuine and Doddridge and Macknight kept it.

schools.summary: Chrysostom watches Paul's tact, taking refuge in David and Isaiah so as not to seem to accuse his nation himself, and hears the clause about those who obtained as an argument from example that leaves no excuse; he adds that naming them the chosen shows the grace from above and their own eagerness together, and does not deny free will. Theodoret places a stop after the opening question and reads Israel as having missed the mark by clinging to the law against its own intent.

Calvin reads the question as put in feigned doubt so the answer may land harder, and finds the proof in the comparison — if Israel gained nothing by merit, what did others gain whose case was no better? He allows the abstract noun to stand for the elect provided more is heard in it than that, and holds that all who are not chosen must remain hardened, the beginning of the reprobate's ruin being that God forsakes them. He then raises the difficulty against himself, that the passages he is about to quote all present hardening as punishment for crimes already committed, and answers that reprobation is the root and the punishing blindness the fruit; his editor rejects the answer as going beyond the Apostle's evident meaning.
Wesley makes the cause of the hardening their own wilful prejudice.

Barnes keeps to what the verse states: the rest were hardened, with nothing said about how it was done, whereas of the election it is expressly said to be of God. Ellicott calls BLINDED an erroneous rendering arising from a confusion of two similar words, gives HARDENED as correct, extends the correction to three other places, and notes the term was medical, used of the forming of chalkstone. Robertson keeps to the covering of thick skin.

debates: Whether the hardening is decretal or punitive. Calvin traces it to reprobation before the foundation of the world and treats the prophetic contexts as fruit rather than root; his own editor answers that the prophets uniformly make hardening a punishment for previous impenitence, and that only the question why some were hardened belongs to the will of God. Wesley makes it wilful prejudice; Barnes declines to state a mode at all.

Whether the word means blinded or hardened. Ellicott calls the received rendering an error from two similar words and corrects it in four places; Barnes allows both, tracing the term to a callus and to a growth in the eye.
outliers: Chrysostom insists the language does not deny free will, taking the chosen to display divine grace and human eagerness together.

schools.summary: Theodoret denies the agency outright: GAVE means gave up, that is, permitted, since God could not inflict infidelity and then require vengeance for it, and the prophet's fuller wording says their eyes THEY have closed.

Calvin refuses to call it the spirit of giddiness and insists on compunction — the bitterness of gall showing itself, a fury in rejecting the truth — so that what is described is active malice rather than torpor. He also sees Paul forestalling the objection that the prophecy was discharged in its own age, the closing words extending the blindness to the coming of Christ.

Clarke holds both ends at once: they wilfully shut their eyes, and God in judgment gave them up to slumber, so that the word which should have woken them became a savour of death. Wesley says the Spirit was at length withdrawn.

Barnes identifies the composite sources, notes the words follow neither Hebrew nor Greek exactly, and wants the milder sense of the disputed noun, whatever benumbs the faculties. Ellicott traces the word's curious history through two unconnected roots and explains how a sharp wound came to mean stupor. Lightfoot states the difficulty and charges the Greek translators with framing senses of their own foreign to the Hebrew. Robertson accepts the finished sense and guesses that the torpor is the result of too much sensation, dulled by incitement into apathy.

debates: How much divine agency the verb carries. Calvin has the reprobate demented by a secret judgment; Theodoret makes GAVE mean permitted and insists no other has blinded them; Clarke holds both, wilful blindness answered by judicial abandonment.

What the disputed noun means. Lightfoot charges the translators with bending a word for compunction into one for stupor; Ellicott derives the sense through the bewilderment following a blow; Barnes settles for insensibility, Calvin for compunction proper.

schools.summary: Theodoret hears in the table their luxurious living, prophesied to be exchanged for its opposite.

Gill has Christ speaking by the mouth of David, the psalm being a prophecy of the Messiah, and on that footing denies the words are imprecations at all, calling them predictions of what should befall the nation for giving the Messiah gall and vinegar. Calvin faces the propriety of such a prayer directly, collecting the cases on both sides and resolving that circumstances make the difference — the rule for men is to bless, and cursing individuals is permitted to none but those inspired to know who has been finally given up.

Clarke reasons from their present temper that what fell on the disobedient before will fall again, their blessings turned to curses, and puts the cause in a sentence: they would have a worldly Messiah, and so rejected the one whose kingdom was not of this world. Wesley notes the imprecation fits Judas as well, and that here sin is punished by sin.

Barnes sets the Hebrew, Greek and Aramaic forms side by side to show the sense kept and the letter not, reads the table as food and the security that goes with it, and converts the question of propriety into one of prediction: what matters is that Paul treats the words as prophecy, and that the prophecy had come true. Ellicott doubts the psalm was David's, taking the name to stand for the Psalter, and finds one of the four words wanting in both Hebrew and Greek. Robertson keeps the four nouns separate and technical.

debates: Whether the words are imprecation or prediction. Gill and Barnes read them as prophecy — Barnes explicitly declining to judge the prayer — while Calvin treats them as a genuine imprecation and defends its lawfulness by the speaker's inspiration.
Whether David wrote the psalm. Ellicott thinks it highly improbable and takes the name for the book; the others quote it as David's without demur.
outliers: Calvin reports Grotius taking the table for the guests who share it, and finds the reading striking since the confederates of the Jews turned enemies and effected their ruin.

schools.summary: Gill denies the darkening is literal, making it the understanding darkened so that they could see no beauty in Christ, and presses it past the spiritual into the civil: the things belonging to their own peace were hid too, and never did a people act more imprudently for its own welfare.

Clarke insists the mood is misread, the words being declarative and not imprecatory — God stating what will be the case of such unbelievers rather than asking for it, their backs bowed in subjection until they acknowledge Jesus as Messiah.

Barnes gives the Hebrew as LET THEIR LOINS TOTTER and uses the verse to open the larger question of the imprecatory psalms, holding that David was not a perfect man and the Spirit of inspiration is not answerable for his imperfections, that all inspiration requires is that such things be recorded as they are, and that many such petitions may be innocent either as a magistrate's prayer for justice or as predictions of what sin brings. Ellicott glosses both halves as figures for one condition and quotes Perowne on the Hebrew idiom. Robertson calls it a terrible imprecation and finds in the second verb the bending of captives under a load.

debates: Whether the sentence asks or announces. Clarke holds the words declarative and not imprecatory; Robertson calls them a terrible imprecation; Barnes takes the apostle to be reading them as prediction while allowing that many such petitions in the Psalms were simply wrong.
outliers: Barnes's account of inspiration — that a recorded prayer may be sinful and the record still inspired — is the fullest statement of the principle anywhere in the chapter.

schools.summary: Theodoret keeps to the history: the gospel was carried to them first, and only when they set themselves against it was it offered to the nations, a sequence framed to sting the gainsayers by letting them see the last made first.

Gill puts the objection in an adversary's mouth with its sharpest edge: if the stumbling was appointed, is God not doing what he forbids in others, laying a stumbling block before the blind? Calvin supplies the key he thinks the argument turns on, that Paul speaks now of the nation as a whole and now of individuals — those who stumbled at Christ fell into destruction, but the nation had not fallen — and illustrates the provoking by a wife put away who is moved by the sight of her successor to seek reconciliation.

Clarke refuses the causal reading altogether: the calling of the Gentiles was God's purpose from the first and implied in the covenant with Abraham, and would have stood whether Israel believed or not, since unbelief in one people could never produce faith in another; what the obstinacy did was accelerate what was already resolved. Wesley catches the lightness of the noun, calling it a slip, a very soft word in the original.

Barnes distinguishes the two verbs — striking the foot against an obstacle against pitching over it beyond recovery — and lists the ways the rejection opened the door, including the destruction of the temple, the scattering of Jewish believers, and the clearing of the apostles' view of the Mosaic institutions. Ellicott finds the cause of the apathy in the privileges themselves. Robertson notes the first verb appears only here in Paul and warns how much depends on whether the conjunction is taken as purpose.

debates: Whether the fall caused the calling of the Gentiles. Barnes lists it as the occasion and traces five effects; Clarke denies causation outright, holding the calling was purposed from the first and merely accelerated by Jewish refusal.

schools.summary: Theodoret argues from the smaller case: if a believing minority brought the riches of divine knowledge to the nations, all the more would the whole, when those who now oppose join in the preaching instead.

Gill settles the term, THE WORLD meaning the Gentiles, since the Jews called themselves the church and all the nations about them the world. Calvin explains why the argument was needed — lest Gentiles dislike the prospect of Jewish salvation as though their own standing depended on Jewish ruin — and denies that the gospel needed the refusal to reach the nations, since Jewish faith would have borne far more fruit than Jewish unbelief occasioned.

Clarke warns that the word rendered FALL here is not the word so rendered in the previous verse, citing Homer twice for the harder verb as used of men killed in battle, and makes the difference the argument: the earlier fall is ruinous, this one a lapse a man can be raised from. Wesley finds it surprising that any Christian doubts the event, takes the survival of the Jews as a distinct people for a standing confirmation, and expects the restoration to convince thousands settled in unbelief and to carry the gospel swiftly to Muslims and heathen.

Barnes traces the word for fulness through its ordinary uses and grounds the expected recovery on what the nation already is — scattered through all nations, knowing the languages, and proved fit for the work since the gospel was first spread by Jews. Ellicott hears a military figure in the first noun, the reduction of a people to a remnant, and sets against it the full complement of the nation with not one missing.

debates: Whether the two words for falling are the same. Clarke separates them on philological grounds and makes the distinction carry the argument; the others treat the second as simply the counterpart of the fulness.
outliers: Wesley's forecast is the most concrete in the chapter, naming the classes of unbeliever the restoration would convince and adding that the heathen would probably have received the gospel long ago had they met only real Christians.

schools.summary: Gill explains that the Roman church held Jews and Gentiles together, so Paul turns from one to the other as his argument requires. Calvin takes the verb in the sense he thinks scripture usually gives it, not to esteem highly but to make illustrious, and reads the sentence as binding the two salvations together: though specially charged with the Gentiles, Paul discharges that office faithfully when he gains any of his own nation.

Clarke would set this verse and the next in a parenthesis and calls the received rendering very improper, since the Greek says I HONOUR THIS MY MINISTRY and to magnify anything but God suggests stretching past the truth. Wesley says that far from being ashamed of ministering to the Gentiles he glories in it.

Barnes explains why the title belongs to Paul in particular — not because others did not preach to Gentiles, but because his commission, his work and his charge were theirs — and turns the phrase into a rule, that a man may not magnify himself but may magnify his office. Ellicott wants the punctuation and particles reset by the amended text and hears a second thought behind the first. Robertson confirms the phrase is qualitative rather than temporal and adds the wish that every minister of Christ glorified his ministry.

debates: How to render the verb. Clarke calls MAGNIFY improper and gives HONOUR; Robertson renders GLORIFY; Calvin takes it as making illustrious rather than esteeming highly.

schools.summary: Theodoret ties the two halves of the ministry into one motion and glosses MY FLESH as naming men who in spirit stood at a distance, related to him only by the tie of kindred.

Gill puts the whole aim of Paul's Gentile labour in one clause, that he might stir his own people to imitate them in seeking Christ. Calvin stops at the startling verb, allowing that a minister is in some way said to save those he brings to faith, and hedging it on both sides — the whole efficacy depends on God, and preaching really is the instrument by which the faithful are saved.
Clarke draws the consequence for the chapter's doctrine: these were all among the rejected, and yet the apostle plainly supposed none of them irrecoverably shut out from the divine favour.

Barnes describes the unwelcome means — unpleasant truths, alarm, the sight of Gentile privilege — and builds from them a short theory that truth irritates, irritation excites attention, and thought once excited may end in conversion; then fences it, since anger is a bad emotion and no wise man raises a storm he may need infinite power to quiet. He also defends the breadth of means, Paul being full of devices.

outliers: Barnes both recommends provocation as a method and rules anger out as an object, holding that if men can be won without it that is better.

schools.summary: Theodoret takes the words literally: if all these were willing to believe, nothing would remain to be accomplished but the resurrection of the dead, and he grounds it on the saying that the gospel shall be preached in all the world and then the end shall come.

Gill identifies the casting away as God writing LO-AMMI over that people and taking the gospel from them. Calvin calls the passage one many find obscure and some awfully pervert, and tests it by the balance of the sentence: since the rejection was reconciliation to the Gentiles, the receiving must be life from the dead to the Gentiles too, so the phrase describes a revival of religion in a decayed Gentile world and not the resurrection at the end.

Clarke asks the Gentile reader to want the restoration as he would want a friend back from the gates of death, treats their survival as a distinct people as collateral proof, and expects the fulfilment of ancient prophecy to convert multitudes who now deny revelation. Wesley reads the phrase as overflowing life to a world that was dead.

Barnes settles reconciliation as the pacifying of parties at variance and reads the closing phrase as a figure, explaining the need for one from the shape of Paul's sentences, since to say the recovery would convert the world would be tame after what he had already said. Robertson leaves the question open and reports the state of it, noting that many think the general resurrection is meant, which is possibly so but by no means certain. Ellicott treats the reconversion as the signal inaugurating the reign of eternal life which the resurrection ushers in.

debates: Whether LIFE FROM THE DEAD is figure or forecast. Barnes and Wesley read a figure of moral revival, and Calvin argues from the balance of the sentence that it must describe the Gentiles rather than the Jews, naming and rejecting the patristic reading; Theodoret and Ellicott take it of the resurrection itself, and Robertson leaves it undecided.

schools.summary: Gill reports and sets aside the reading that takes both figures of Christ, and is harder on the one that runs a hereditary holiness down from Abraham, since none such reached Ishmael; his own answer is the early Jewish converts. Calvin levels the comparison first, nation against nation and not man against man, and insists the holiness is external and relative rather than personal, conferred on a race and not on persons, so that the Jews were sanctified in their father; he closes by calling the dignity of an elect people a strictly supernatural privilege.

Clarke takes both firstfruits at once, Abraham's conversion and the Jews who have now embraced Christianity, and defines HOLY carefully as consecrated and set apart to sacred use. Wesley reads the verse forward, the consecration of the firstfruits being reckoned the consecration of all, so that a few converted Jews are the earnest of the rest.

Barnes explains the rite behind the figure, a cake of dough offered before the mass could be used, and settles the firstfruit as the patriarchs, hearing behind the second image the prophet's green olive tree. Robertson notes the Greek follows the wording of that law, ventures that the root may be Abraham singly, and recalls the double sense of Israel. Ellicott adds the ceremony of the heave offering and expects the latter end of Israel to be like its beginning.

debates: Who the firstfruit is. Gill reports the reading that takes it of Christ and rejects it, and settles on the first Jewish converts; Clarke takes both converts and patriarchs; Barnes, Robertson, Ellicott and Calvin settle on the patriarchs.

What kind of holiness passes. Calvin makes it external and federal, transmissible with the covenant's rights but not with faith; Gill denies any holiness derived from Abraham to his natural seed at all.

schools.summary: Gill limits the breaking off by chronology: it cannot be exclusion from the national church, since the men meant were that church, nor the destruction of the nation, since nation and temple still stood when Paul wrote, but their being left outside the gospel church gathered among them. Calvin notices how carefully the severity is moderated — not the top of the tree cut off but some branches broken — and holds that Paul's object was not to describe usual gardening but to frame a comparison fit for his purpose, inverting nature by making the stock good and the graft bad.

Wesley makes the inversion the force of the warning: even had the graft been nobler than the stock, its dependence for life and nourishment would leave it no room to boast, and how much less when the wild olive is grafted into the good.

Barnes describes both trees from a naturalist's account, the cultivated olive and the smaller barren wild one, and reads the figure as a fruitless church made vigorous. Robertson reports Ramsay's finding that the ancients really did graft a wild-olive shoot onto an old olive to reinvigorate it, and sets against it Paul's own words a few verses on that the procedure is contrary to nature. Ellicott prefers AMONG THEM of the branches generally and reports a textual question in the closing phrase, three weighty manuscripts omitting the second connective.

debates: Whether the horticulture is real. Robertson cites evidence that the wild-olive graft was actually practised to reinvigorate an old tree; Calvin holds it was not done except where the good tree was failing, and that the apostle did not care; Wesley calls it contrary to human practice outright.
Where the new branches were put. Calvin renders IN THEIR STEAD with Beza, Pareus and Macknight; Grotius has BETWEEN THEM and Doddridge AMONG THEM, which Ellicott prefers.

schools.summary: Theodoret supplies a key to the whole allegory, understanding by the firstfruit Christ in his human nature, by the root Abraham, by the branches the Jewish people, and by the richness of the olive the doctrines of religion.

Gill turns the prohibition into a positive duty — not merely refraining from vaunting but pitying, praying, and being humbled under a sense of the grace that settled a wild olive in a gospel church — and denies any difference at all between believing Gentile and believing Jew. Calvin names the person the Gentiles would be quarrelling with: they cannot contend about race without contending with Abraham, who is the root that bears them, and adds that when Christ pulled down the partition wall the world came into a favour conferred beforehand on a chosen people.

Clarke turns the argument toward the despised themselves — you have brought no blessing on the Jewish people, but through that very people all your blessings came. Wesley makes it a question with an edge on it, aimed past the first century: do not those do this very thing who despise the Jews, or deny their future conversion?

Robertson hears in the imperative a command to stop a habitual fault rather than a caution against a possible one, and notes the emphatic position of the pronoun. Barnes states the arithmetic of the figure and draws out what it commits Paul to, that the church is one and the Christian dispensation a prolongation of the old, since a tree keeps its identity when branches are exchanged. Ellicott states it in a line: the privileges are derived and not original.

outliers: Wesley extends the boast beyond contempt to doctrine, treating the denial of a future Jewish conversion as itself a form of boasting against the branches.

schools.summary: Calvin takes the objector's plea and turns it round: if the cutting off was through unbelief and the grafting by faith, the Gentile's business is to acknowledge a favour and keep his mind low, since it belongs to faith to generate humility and fear. He describes a fear held together with assurance — the misery of our nature yielding dread and weariness, which yet do not keep the mind from resting calm on God's goodness — and answers the charge that such a warning unsettles salvation by distinguishing the address to the whole Gentile body from any word to individuals.
Clarke states the objector's case bluntly: God was displeased with them, cast them out, and took you in their place.

Robertson calls the speaker presumptuous and hears contempt for the cast-off Jews in the very shape of the sentence. Barnes reconstructs the reasoning fairly from what Paul had already said, and anticipates the answer, that this was not why they were rejected.

debates: Whether the verse teaches that faith may fail. Calvin's editors call that an entire misapprehension, since what is in view is the Gentile world and not the individual, professed faith and not living, outward privilege and not inward change; they cite Augustine on perseverance and Pareus on temporary faith.

schools.summary: Theodoret puts it as a simple exchange — unbelief made them aliens from the root, faith connected you with it — and concludes that it becomes you not to grow self-sufficient but to fear and tremble.
Gill describes the manoeuvre from the other side: the breaking off and the grafting are granted, and what is quietly denied is that the one happened for the sake of the other.

Clarke works the consequence out in a chain — received by faith, therefore not by works; not by works, therefore no merit; and therefore mere mercy — and makes the parallel uncomfortable, since it is as possible for you to be unfaithful as it was for them. Wesley fastens on the conditionality, both clauses being conditional and not absolute, since had they been absolute there would have been room to boast, and adds that the faith itself is God's free gift.

Robertson thinks the opening word perhaps ironical and notes both datives are instrumental. Barnes reads the reply as a piece of argumentative tact worth studying, defines the fear as humility and watchfulness rather than terror, draws three lessons from it, and states the practical upshot without hedging: the continuance of these mercies depends on fidelity.

debates: How much assent the opening word carries. Robertson suspects irony; Barnes and Gill take it as a real concession given a slight turn toward the truth.

schools.summary: Theodoret makes the argument turn on character rather than descent: the connection of nature profited them nothing once they no longer kept the same disposition.

Gill catalogues what made the Jews the greater case — natural descendants, a national church state, a national adoption in which they were called God's firstborn, and Christ their own according to the flesh. Calvin calls this the most powerful thing yet said against self-confidence, describes its proper effect physically, and puts their ruin in a clause, that through supine dependence on the dignity they had obtained they despised what God appointed; he also takes the verse as evidence that the address is to the body of the Gentiles, since excision cannot touch men whose election is unchangeable.

Clarke presses the warning into self-examination, telling the Gentile to remember the rock he was hewn from and the pit he was dug out of, and to depend without ceasing on free grace. Wesley guards the fear from being mistaken in a line: it is not opposed to trust, but to pride and security.

Barnes adds the point that stings, that God may be quite as ready to reject a grafted branch as one of the parent stock. Robertson translates the opening command as a demand to stop something already happening. Ellicott judges it better to drop the words rendered TAKE HEED LEST, leaving the flatter statement that neither will he spare you.

outliers: Ellicott's preferred text removes the warning's softening clause, so that the sentence states the outcome rather than urging vigilance against it.

schools.summary: Gill takes the pairing itself to be the lesson, since holding grace toward some and strict justice toward others in one view is what abates pride. Calvin dramatises the warning as a speech — think first what you were, then what you are now — and names the event that proved it necessary, the later defection of a world God had watered with grace almost in a moment, after which the treasure of salvation was taken away.

Clarke turns the metaphor into a manual, writing as a man who has performed the operation himself, and reads Paul's two nouns as the halves of one gardener's action; he then runs the figure forward, the tree cut down but not rooted up, and the Gentile branch's standing bound up with the survival of the people through whom the covenant came. Wesley makes the threatened excision final.

Henry, observing that spiritual judgments are the sorest of all, argues the restoration from the harder case already granted, that Israel's return is less improbable than that Gentiles should have been made children of Abraham at all; and he is careful what a restoration would mean, not priesthood and temple and ceremonies but belief in Christ and one sheepfold under one shepherd.

Barnes insists SEVERITY has been misheard, the Greek noun belonging to the gardener trimming decayed branches and conveying no idea of injustice; he notes the possessive in HIS GOODNESS is not in the Greek, states that obedience is the indispensable condition of continuing favour without being its merit, and names the churches that lost what they had. Robertson confirms the derivation and marks the closing verb as a plain future passive. Lightfoot, prefacing his own work on the chapter, asks whether the nation was not blinded and cast off before the murder of Christ, since they were a generation of vipers when the Baptist appeared.

debates: When the casting off began. Lightfoot unsettles the usual chronology by asking whether the nation was not already blinded before the crucifixion, against the common dating from that crime.
What a restoration would restore. Henry rules out priesthood, temple and ceremonies, to all of which an end has been put, and leaves only belief in Christ and union with the Gentiles.

schools.summary: Theodoret makes the symmetry a matter of justice rather than ease — it becomes God's righteousness both to sever the ungrateful graft and to rejoin those who renounce unbelief — and notes with approval that the same word for grafting is used of both.

Gill agrees the restoration is possible and doubts it will happen unaided, holding that they lie under an ignorance nothing can overcome and must and will abide in unbelief unless the Spirit convinces them and they are powerfully drawn. Calvin explains why the appeal to power persuades only some — to the profane it is frigid, since they view God's power at a distance and rob it of effect, while the faithful see it presently at work — and adds that reversing the present arrangement is easier than establishing it was.

Clarke presses the point about ability further, holding that God has furnished them with all the means necessary for faith so that they may believe whenever they will, and that the veil on their heart is not one God spread but one their own obstinacy occasioned.

Barnes makes the negative condition the hinge, since unbelief was the sole cause of the rejection and its removal removes the cause, and reads the verse as establishing both that God has the power and that he has not bound himself to exclude them for ever. Robertson calls the statement that God is able the crux of the whole matter and lets it stand.

debates: Whether the Jews can turn. Clarke holds they may believe whenever they will, the veil being self-imposed; Gill holds they must and will abide in unbelief unless the Spirit convinces them and they are drawn.
themes: if they abide not in unbelief

schools.summary: Theodoret makes the contrast concrete by naming what the wild olive lacked: no law tending it, no prophets watering and pruning and taking the needful care.
Gill reads the sequence as an argument in two steps, the previous verse establishing the restoration from God's power and this one its likelihood from what has already been done in the Gentiles.

Clarke assembles the evidence that the wild olive's barrenness was proverbial, and draws a point about the phrase describing it: BY NATURE means not naturally barren so much as customarily left uncultivated, as the answering phrase means contrary to all custom. He then argues from the lowest description of the Gentile side, men without God and atheists in the world, that the change is far more probable in a people who acknowledge the one true God. Wesley states the inversion in a sentence.

Barnes puts the argument as one from the harder case to the easier, insists the figure makes no claim about physical constitution but about habits and thoughts, and lists what a Jewish hearer already has that a heathen one did not — one God, the authority of revelation, the Scriptures, an expected Messiah, and a settled habit of reverence. Robertson keeps the other half of the sense, that the point is God's power to do what natural processes do not.

themes: the argument from the harder case

schools.summary: Theodoret defines a mystery as a thing known only to those entrusted with it, and expects the believing of the rest to follow the coming of Elijah, who shall restore all things.

Calvin adds the pastoral reason for the disclosure, that it both checks Gentile arrogance and keeps the defection of the Jews from unsettling weak minds; he presses its use against despair, since the manner of their conversion will be neither common nor usual and measuring it by our own judgment is absurd, and takes the fulness for a great number on the ground that Gentiles would form almost the whole body of the Church.

Clarke goes to the etymology of MYSTERY and resists any reading that makes the restoration wait on an absolute completion: the word need not mean every nation and every individual, nor need the coming in mean what is usually understood by conversion, and his warning is blunt, that on the stricter reading we shall wait for ever. Wesley names two forms the forbidden conceit takes, dreaming you are the only church, or that the church of Rome cannot fail.

Barnes insists the word carries no suggestion of the unintelligible, only of what was concealed and is now disclosed, reads IN PART as partial and no more with deliberate silence about which part and how long, and argues that the two conversions are likely intermingled and perhaps simultaneous, so Christians may work for both at once. Ellicott says the word never means something withheld from all but a few, and attaches the qualifying phrase to ISRAEL. Robertson denies the pagan sense of an esoteric doctrine for initiates and attaches the phrase to the verb instead.

debates: What IN PART qualifies. Robertson attaches it to the verb, Ellicott to ISRAEL, Barnes leaves it deliberately vague; Calvin denies it refers to time or number at all and makes it a softening, which his editor rejects since the clause that follows supplies a limit.

How full the fulness of the Gentiles must be. Clarke denies it requires every nation and every individual, or conversion in the stricter sense; Calvin takes it for a great number; Barnes denies the Jews must wait on its completion at all.

schools.summary: Gill names and rejects the reading that takes Israel here for the mystical Israel of Jews and Gentiles, and describes what he expects in the prophets' language — a nation born again at once, coming up out of the lands where they were scattered, appointing one head, and acknowledging Jesus as the true Messiah. Calvin takes the opposite side deliberately, extending the word to all the people of God gathered from both, with the Jews holding first place as the firstborn, and appeals to the phrase used at the close of Galatians.

Clarke separates the second question from the first: SAVED cannot mean eternal glory, since no one can suppose every Jew then living taken into it, and in scripture applied to that people it means being gathered out of the nations and made his peculiar people. Wesley makes the tense his whole comment — the deliverer is come already, but not yet the full fruit of his coming.

Barnes divides the same way, adds the rabbinic maxim Paul turns to his own use, and observes that the time is among the things kept in the Father's own power, the concealment being deliberate lest we relax our efforts. Ellicott calls the change from TO Zion to OUT OF Zion a curious variation and explains it as quotation from memory, adding that the Messiah must take up his abode there before he can issue from it. Robertson lays both readings of ALL ISRAEL out, declines to choose, and commits only to praying for the conversion of Jews as a whole.

debates: What ALL ISRAEL means. Gill insists on the Jewish nation as a body; Calvin extends it to the whole people of God gathered from Jews and Gentiles; Robertson sets the two readings side by side and declines.
What SAVED means here. Clarke restricts it to being gathered out of the nations and made a peculiar people; Barnes reads it as recovery to divine favour and conversion to Christ.

schools.summary: Theodoret argues that since the law punishes transgressors rather than forgiving them, the remission in view must be the one that arises from baptism, and understands by all Israel those who believe, whether descended from Israel naturally or joined to him by the kinship of faith.

Gill draws the plainest inference from the word COVENANT, that what God has promised there will not be broken, so the conversion of the Jews is not merely possible or probable but certain. Calvin explains why the clause about taking sins away was needed just here, since what had been said of so stubborn a people might have seemed incredible, and the stumbling block is removed by showing the covenant included a free remission of sins.

Clarke prints the prophet's words at length to show how greatly the quotation has been compressed, proposes reading these two verses as a parenthesis since the sentence about the mystery joins directly to the one about enmity, and collects some two dozen passages from the prophets that seem to him to point to a restoration of the Jewish commonwealth.

Barnes takes the second half as an abridgement of the new-covenant promise in Jeremiah and is as concerned to say what it does not contain — not that the Redeemer will come in person and preach to them, nor that they will be restored to the land — expecting instead a conversion worked by human means and prayer, so that the Gentiles repay the labour of the ancient Jews. Ellicott traces the clause instead to the Greek of a passage in Isaiah, where the same two elements appear. Robertson renders the possessive strictly as the covenant proceeding from God, and marks the deliverance as religious and ethical rather than political.

debates: Where the second half of the citation comes from. Barnes and Calvin abridge it from Jeremiah's new-covenant promise; Ellicott traces it to the Greek of Isaiah, on the strength of two shared elements.
What the promise does not include. Barnes rules out both a personal preaching visit and a restoration to the land; Clarke gathers the prophetic passages that seem to promise a restored commonwealth.

schools.summary: Theodoret puts the double relation as a movement of the eye: looking at the Gentiles he was charged to teach, he counts these men enemies; turning to their forefathers, and remembering that God chose them out of the whole earth, he finds that on their account he loves even these.

Calvin turns the clause about Gentile advantage into a rebuke, since the worst thing about the Jews ought not to expose them to contempt: their chief crime was itself the means by which the way to the gospel was opened, and they were blinded for a time by a providence that had the Gentiles in view — while God remained mindful of the covenant by which he testified that he loved that nation according to his eternal purpose.

Clarke states the position in terms of privilege, the grace that overturned their peculiarity being exactly what they resent, while with respect to the original choosing they remain beloved for their forefathers' sake. Wesley refuses to choose whose enemies they are and adds a third party, making them enemies to the gospel, to God, and to themselves.

Barnes sets the two descriptions opposite each other and guards the sentence against two misreadings — that God approves their conduct, and that the promise rests on the fathers' merit — adding that no one has any guarantee of favour except by complying with the explicit terms of mercy. Robertson makes the grammatical observation that settles both terms, each adjective being passive. Ellicott states the whole position in two strokes, the estrangement suffered to make room for the Gentiles and the original choice not thereby abrogated.

debates: Whose enemies they are. Calvin's editors collect the answers — of Paul and the Church, of the gospel, of God — and weigh the parallel with BELOVED as favouring the last; Wesley adds that they are enemies to themselves.

schools.summary: Theodoret reads the verse against all of this and argues from cases: God does resume the blessings he gives when he sees ingratitude, as with Saul, with Solomon, and with the Jews bereaved of the prophets' guardianship — so the sentence is an incitement rather than an unconditional guarantee.

Gill settles which gifts are meant by elimination, excluding the gifts of nature and providence which God gives and withdraws, and the external gifts that qualify men for public service, which the parable of the talents shows may be taken away; what remains is the special grace given to God's elect in Christ before the world was. Calvin restricts the promise the other way, reading the two nouns as one idea, the gift of calling, and referring it to the adoption of Abraham's posterity into covenant, so that the point is a national adoption not cut up by the roots.
Clarke defines repentance as applied to God as a change of purpose relative to declarations made subject to conditions, and refers the reader to the passage where God explains that principle himself.

Barnes insists the clause says nothing of man's repentance but only that God does not change his purpose, gathers the texts that state this of him, and draws the consequences plainly, since to renew a soul and then leave it to ruin would suppose exactly the change the verse denies. Robertson is the most exact: the Greek word is built on a verb meaning to be sorry afterwards, not on the word for changing one's mind. Ellicott catches both senses in a phrase, not to be revoked and not even to be regretted.

debates: How wide the promise runs. Calvin restricts it to the national adoption; his editor prefers an ascent from the promises to the calling they came from, and reports others extending it to faith, remission, sanctification and perseverance, with the corollary that no Gentile nation once favoured will be wholly forsaken.

Whether the promise is unconditional. Barnes reads it as securing that none of God's true friends are cast off; Theodoret cites Saul, Solomon and the Jews themselves as cases where gifts were resumed, and points to the threat made to the Gentiles a few verses earlier.
outliers: Theodoret alone treats the verse as an incitement addressed to the Jews rather than a guarantee, and turns its own chapter's warning against the unconditional reading.

schools.summary: Gill fills in the period appealed to — the times of ignorance and idolatry when God suffered the nations to walk in their own ways while the Jews held his oracles and statutes — and describes the unbelief as a range rather than one error, from denying that there is a God at all to serving many.

Clarke will not let the connection stay merely chronological: what brought the Gentiles in was the method by which God destroyed the Jewish peculiarity and fulfilled the Abrahamic covenant, and that same method occasioned the unbelief and obstinate opposition of the Jews, since it was the removal of their distinctness they could not bear.

Barnes reads the clause as a plain reference to the former idolatrous condition of the heathen world and notes the verb may as well be rendered HAVE NOT OBEYED. Robertson supports the double rendering from the word itself, which means to disbelieve and then to disobey, and points out how heavily the sentence leans on its adverb, NOW occurring three times.

outliers: Clarke makes the two halves of the verse one act of God seen from two sides, so that the same measure which admitted the Gentiles provoked the Jewish opposition.

schools.summary: Theodoret will not let the purpose clause be pressed: the Jews did not disbelieve in order that they might find mercy, but disbelieved from hardness of heart and will find mercy by turning; and he grounds the hope on the precedent of Gentiles blessed after a long ungodliness.

Gill flags the construction before anything else, since in the Greek the words about mercy attach to the first clause, and offers three ways of taking that reading; the English follows Beza, who follows Theophylact, in joining them to what comes after.

Clarke states the argument as a chain whose force lies in the parallel — as surely as the Jews were once in and the Gentiles out, and as surely as the Gentiles are now in and the Jews out, so surely will the Jews be brought back — and names what will change, their consenting to acknowledge the Lord Jesus.

Barnes draws out what the reading commits the church to: conversion by Gentile instrumentality and not by miracle, by the Gentiles' pity, and when great numbers of them have themselves been called in; he then asks whether the time is not approaching for the attempt, admitting frankly that such efforts had so far been unsuccessful. Robertson explains the possessive as objective and standing early for emphasis, and finds in the clause that God's purpose is for the Jews to receive a blessing yet. Ellicott keeps to the mechanism, the sight of mercy to Gentiles acting as a stimulus.

debates: Where the phrase about mercy belongs. Gill notes the Greek attaches it to the first clause and offers three senses on that reading, while the English, following Beza and Theophylact, joins it to the second.

schools.summary: Theodoret says CONCLUDED stands for CONVICTED and works it differently on each side, the Gentiles convicted by natural judgment and by the creation, and the Jews more heavily still, having the prophets besides.

Gill mentions and rejects the gentler figure of sheaves bound by a band, and states God's part flatly: he is not the author of unbelief, does not put it into men or them into it, but finding them in it concludes them there and does not yet say to the prisoners, go forth. Calvin makes the emphasis fall on mercy — God is bound to none and saves freely because all are equally lost — and calls it extremely gross folly to conclude from this that all shall be saved.

Clarke turns the whole into a courtroom running into a jail: both parties tried at God's bar, found guilty, condemned and locked up under the jailer unbelief, and then a general pardon proclaimed by the gospel — welcomed by the Gentiles, refused by the Jews on the terms proposed, and still open.

Barnes traces the verb to men shut in a jail or a besieged city and to fish taken in a net, and works through God's agency in stages, holding that he does not compel men to remain in unbelief but declares that they are in it and hems them about with proof of their need of a Saviour. Robertson gives the same net image, marks the tense as recording a result already reached, and insists THE ALL are those who receive mercy, not that all men are saved. Ellicott takes the sentence furthest, calling it a summary of the whole course of human history and offering it as a motto for the theological side of the theory of evolution.

debates: How God shuts men up in unbelief. Gill and Barnes insist on declaration rather than compulsion; Theodoret reads the verb as convicting; Calvin's editors report Chrysostom's paraphrase that God proved all to be unbelieving, and Pareus's rule that he manifests, accuses and condemns unbelief without effecting or approving it.
outliers: Ellicott reads the verse as a philosophy of history and offers it as a motto for the theological side of evolution, answering the objection about wasted individual life by our seeing only part of God's ways.

schools.summary: Cyril presses the smaller case: if the least of God's works are past comprehension and no one can find a footstep of the Lord, then he who made them all cannot be comprehended. Theodoret adds that the scheme of the divine economy surpasses human understanding, and that not even the invisible powers reach the bottom of it.

Calvin turns the exclamation into a discipline, since a man who had been caught up to the third heaven was at last overcome by the mystery and could only wonder; so a bridle should be set on thought and tongue whenever we enter on the eternal counsels, that our reasoning may end in admiration. Gill takes the outburst as the epilogue of the doctrinal part of the letter, closing everything argued from justification to the restoring of Israel.

Clarke divides the last two words, wisdom belonging to the designs and knowledge to the means, so that the designs are right and the means fittest. Wesley marks the change of scale, Paul having sailed in a narrow sea in the ninth chapter and now being in the ocean, and maps the three nouns onto the verses that follow.

Henry contrasts the shallowness of every other kind of wealth, where one may soon see the bottom, and gives the image the chapter is remembered for — Paul despairing to find the bottom and sitting down at the brink to adore the depth. He distinguishes knowledge as seeing all by one clear view from wisdom as ordering it to God's purposes, and presses the figure of the untraceable path: God leaves no footsteps and makes no track, his ways of providence being new every morning, so that the judgments of his hand are to be adored rather than pried into while the way of our duty stays a high road.

Barnes argues the received rendering makes two objects of admiration where there are three, notes the Syriac and Arabic read so, and takes the metaphor of depth from the unfathomable sea. Ellicott allows either construction and defines riches as inexhaustible resources by which God brings good even out of evil. Robertson sees the posture in the syntax, an argument that has carried Paul to the heights and left him unable to sound the bottom, and identifies the two closing adjectives as rare double compounds, the second borrowed from Job.

debates: How many things are being admired, and how the nouns join. Barnes and the Syriac make three coordinate objects; the Authorised rendering ties wisdom and knowledge under riches; Calvin's editors report the fathers divided, Origen, Chrysostom and Theodoret joining riches to depth and Ambrose and Augustine to wisdom.
themes: adoration as the end of argument

schools.summary: Calvin sets out two reasons for restraining audacity, that mortals are too blind to view predestination by their own understanding and that no one can claim God as debtor, and then guards the caution against weakening the certainty of faith, distinguishing God's secret counsel from his will made known in scripture: access to the latter is open to those who follow the Spirit soberly, while the former has a depth no investigation reaches. Gill approaches from the side of revelation, since the intentions of God's mind could never be known unless disclosed, and even disclosed are known only in part and through a glass darkly.

Clarke reads the verse as a rebuke to a kind of writing and names an instance — a writer who drew out schemes of reprobation and election link by link and closed with this very exclamation about ways past finding out, forgetting that he had just searched them out and offered the diagram as proof.

Barnes gives the point by contrast, since earthly monarchs keep counsellors and God calls in none, and says the quotation is meant to silence opposition and hush complaint. Robertson ends on the same note in a line, that some men seem to feel competent for the job. Ellicott adds the structural observation that the two clauses answer to the wisdom and the knowledge, as the next verse answers to the riches.

debates: How far the caution reaches. Clarke turns it against systematic schemes of decree; Calvin insists it must not be applied so as to weaken assurance, since the faithful do understand the mind of the Lord by the Spirit, and confines the prohibition to the hidden counsel.

schools.summary: Theodoret lays out the pattern, the three questions answering the three nouns in reverse, and finds a tenderness in the arrangement: nothing is really due for anything we first gave, and yet in mercy God condescends to call each free gift a repayment.

Calvin makes the verse a defence of God's righteousness against a specific charge, since unrighteousness could only be alleged if God failed to render each his due, and pushes it past the obvious case: not merely our corrupt nature but even a perfect man could produce nothing, being from the first moment of existence so indebted by the right of creation that he has nothing of his own. Gill runs the same argument down the scale of creatures, from Adam in innocence through the angels to sinful men.

Clarke asks the questions rather than answering them and aims them at the quarrel the chapter has been settling — whether either people has a right to God's blessings, whether he wronged the Jews in choosing the Gentiles — then closes with three of another kind, how the Creator can be indebted to the creature, the cause depend on the effect, or the Father of every good gift be under obligation to those he provides for.

Barnes explains that the old English word for preventing means to anticipate or go before, so the question is who conferred a favour first, and notes the passage adds that whatever is under the whole heaven is God's. Robertson marks the verb as occurring nowhere else in the New Testament and the rendering as Paul's own rather than the Greek version's. Ellicott states the connection briefly, that the means by which God works are not supplied from without.

Theodoret uses the verse against a named party, since Paul recognised no difference between OF WHOM and THROUGH WHOM as marking superiority and inferiority, applying both to one Person — so that Arians and Eunomians are caught whichever Person they assign it to.

Calvin treats the verse as proof of the one before it, since we were created out of nothing and exist through him now, so that our being should be spent on making his glory known; he states the alternative as an absurdity, that the order of nature would be subverted if the beginning of all things were not also the end. Gill applies the three prepositions to grace as well as nature, so that election, redemption and regeneration alike spring from God's will, are brought about by his power, and issue in his glory.

Clarke notices the formula was not unique to Paul, quoting the emperor Marcus Antoninus addressing Nature as God and suggesting he borrowed it from this epistle, and closes on the asymmetry of what can be explained: ten thousand reasons appear why God should display his justice and scarcely one why he should display his mercy, and yet the displays for which no reason can be found are the greater and the more numerous. Wesley compresses the three into Creator, Preserver and ultimate end.

Robertson names them Source, Agent and Goal and reports Alford's verdict on the doxology. Barnes assigns the three the same roles, denies that the end is God's happiness or any addition to him, and closes the letter's argument with observations on the creator's right, on humility, and on a universe fitted to declare his glory. Ellicott calls it a mistake to find an allusion to the Trinity here, the subject being God the Father and the prominent idea the unity of creation.

debates: Whether the three prepositions carry a Trinitarian sense. Ellicott calls that a mistake here, taking the subject to be the Father and the idea the unity of creation, while granting that elsewhere such prepositions express the threefold relation; Theodoret uses their application to one Person as an argument against Arian and Eunomian distinctions.
themes: of him, through him, to him
